prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When God appears before me he is a burning woman tied to a bush. Her nakedness, a missed spot on a busy canvas, where a male hand has been practicing female gestures. For instance, hanging herself like laundry over her own arm. Nipple-colons introduce this scene of medieval war: horses crowned with riders are leaving; horses’ tails, like a clock’s hands, whip flies of hours off their round thighs. Time is an insect that leaves its maggots to hatch on an open wound of a mammal. There’s more face on these thighs than on all of the women’s bodies. One, with an arrow aimed at her, hands on her bent knees as if she wanted to ski into death like a scared child, mocks the splendid horse tails with hair so red, all of her blood must have gone into it. So, it isn’t a bush on fire. It’s red hair she used as a shield. In the distance, a town burning. Impatiently, horses whip buzzing ashes. The end.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, God, Her

outputs.L1: When God appears before me, He takes the form of a burning woman bound to a bush. Her nakedness is a missed spot on a crowded canvas, where a male hand has been rehearsing female gestures—draping her, for instance, like laundry over her own arm. Nipples, like colons, introduce this scene of medieval war: horses crowned with riders are departing; their tails, like the hands of a clock, whip the flies of passing hours from their rounded thighs. Time is an insect that leaves its maggots to hatch in the open wound of a mammal. There is more face upon these thighs than on all the women's bodies combined. One woman, an arrow trained upon her, rests her hands on her bent knees as though she meant to ski into death like a frightened child; she mocks the splendid horsetails with hair so red that all her blood must have drained into it. And so it is not a bush aflame—it is the red hair she has raised as a shield. In the distance, a town is burning. Impatiently, the horses whip at the buzzing ash. The end.
outputs.L2: The moment God materializes before me, She takes the form of a woman aflame, bound to a shrub. Her bare body is like an overlooked gap on a crowded canvas, the place where a masculine hand rehearsed feminine poses. Consider how she drapes herself, as though she were laundry laid across her own forearm. Her nipples form colons that announce this tableau of warfare from the Middle Ages: horses topped with mounted riders depart the scene; the tails of those horses swing like the hands of a clock, flicking away the fly-hours from their rounded flanks. Time behaves like some insect, depositing its larvae to grow within the raw wound of a mammal. These thighs carry more expression than every woman's figure combined. One woman, an arrow pointed toward her, grips her folded knees as though preparing to glide into death the way a frightened youngster might, and she ridicules the magnificent horse tails with hair so intensely red it seems every drop of her blood was drained to create the color. This means the burning shrub was never a shrub at all. It was crimson hair she wielded for protection. Far off, a town is engulfed in flames. The horses restlessly swat at the humming cinders. The end.

# A Vision of Fire and War

The narrator envisions God not as a distant, abstract presence but as a burning, naked woman tied to a bush—her form flickering with flame. This image emerges through a male hand imitating female gestures, as if masculine expression could only approach the divine by mimicking the feminine, reaching toward something it cannot fully possess or embody.

Around this central figure unfolds a scene of medieval war. Horses bearing armored riders are departing the field, their tails swishing rhythmically behind them. The motion recalls the hands of a clock, sweeping away the hours—each swish marking time's relentless passage, as though the very act of retreat measures the minutes bleeding from the day.

Time itself takes on a grotesque, organic form. It is likened to an insect that deposits its maggots into the open wound of a mammal, where they hatch and feed. Here, the passing of hours becomes something parasitic and consuming, breeding within living flesh, turning injury into a nursery for decay.

The women in this vision speak through their bodies rather than their faces. Their thighs express more emotion than any expression could convey—fear, tension, and vulnerability rendered in the language of posture and flesh. One figure crouches low in terror, her body braced as an arrow takes aim at her, frozen in the instant before impact.

Finally, what first appears to be the burning bush reveals itself as something else entirely: a woman's fiery red hair, raised and held as a shield. Behind her, in the distance, a town stands consumed by flames. The blaze of her hair and the blaze of the burning city echo one another across the landscape, blurring the line between protection and destruction, between the human figure and the world it cannot save.
outputs.L4:
**Ekphrasis: The Burning Field**

Look here, where the panel darkens at its edge, where the varnish has gone amber with centuries—look at what the painter wanted you to see, and then at what he could not help but show.

The horses are leaving. This is the first thing. They turn their long necks away from the frame as if ashamed, their riders already half-dissolved into the smoke that the artist mixed from bone-black and the ground bones of the dead. The animals go with the terrible patience of things that will not be asked to answer for what they carry. Their hooves are the last soft sound. After them, silence, and the crackle of the thing that will not stop burning.

Because the women are on fire.

I want to say it plainly, the way the painting refuses to. Along the middle distance they stand in their rows like saints in a golden ground, except that the gold is not glory but flame, and it climbs them the way ivy climbs a ruined wall—patient, decorative, total. The painter has given each of them a posture: this one lifting her arms, this one bowed, this one with her face turned outward toward us across five hundred years, asking the only question a burning woman can ask. He has rendered the folds of their dresses with such care. He has been so faithful to the way cloth takes light. And that faithfulness is its own small cruelty, because to paint a thing beautifully is, sometimes, to agree with its existence.

Here is what war leaves: the broken cart, the wheel still turning on nothing. The wall reduced to its own diagram. A dog. A shoe. The economy of destruction is that it converts everything into the same gray matter, levels the cathedral and the hovel, the general and the girl who drew his water. Mortality is the great flattener, and the painter knew this, and he arranged his ruin like a still life, so that death might be composed, might be held, might be survived by the eye.

But I keep returning to the figure at the right.

The scholars have called it, for generations, a burning bush. They wrote it in the catalogues. They pointed to the theological precedent, the Moses of it, the God-who-speaks-from-fire, the sign that burns and is not consumed. They found the reference reassuring. It let the flame mean something. It let the panel be about the divine, about revelation, about the covenant between the terrible and the sacred.

But look again.

It is not a bush. It is her hair. It is a woman's red hair, unbound, and she has raised it—or someone has raised it for her—as a shield across her body, this useless coppery flag of the self, this last thing that was hers, held up against the swords and the sparks as though beauty could deflect the blade. As though the very thing the world had prized her for might now, at the end, protect her. It cannot. That is the point the painter buried under his pigment and his piety. Her hair is not a miracle that burns without being consumed. Her hair is simply burning. She is being consumed. And we have spent five centuries calling it scripture so that we would not have to call it what it is.

This is what they made of her: first an ornament, then an offering, then a symbol, then a footnote in a museum. At every stage her body was for something other than herself—for pleasure, for war, for allegory, for the education of the tasteful eye. Even her suffering was requisitioned. Even her death was hung on a wall and lit correctly and admired.

The horses are almost gone now, out past the frame's right edge, into the white margin where painting stops and the world resumes. Soon the last of them will be only a tail, a rumor of motion. And she will still be there. She will always still be there, holding up her red hair against the fire, and the fire will always be about to win, and we will always be standing here, the visitors, the readers of catalogues, deciding what to name the thing so that we can bear to keep looking.

Call it a bush, if you must.

I will call it a woman.
outputs.L5:
# When God Painted Her

When God first thought of gentleness, He paused before creation and imagined *Her*.

She was not an afterthought, nor a decoration upon the world. When the Creator sketched the mountains and set the stars spinning, He saved a special tenderness for the moment He would breathe life into a woman. In Her, He placed the quiet strength that could carry burdens without complaint, and the fierce love that would defend her own against any storm.

**When** the world feels heavy, look closely and you will find Her holding it together—a mother soothing a crying child at midnight, a sister offering her last coin to someone in need, a friend whose words heal wounds that medicine cannot reach.

God knew that strength wears many faces. Sometimes it roars like a lioness protecting her cubs. Other times it whispers, patient and unwavering, like a candle that refuses to go out.

**When** she doubts her worth, may she remember that she was made in the image of something divine. Her hands, though weary, do sacred work. Her heart, though bruised, still chooses to love.

For every time the world tried to make Her feel small, God had already declared Her enough.

And **when** all is said and done, we may finally understand: perhaps the greatest evidence of God's love for the world was the day He decided to create *Her*.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem describing a vision of God as a burning woman tied to a bush, blending medieval war imagery with grotesque and vivid metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Burning Woman Tied to the Bush

She is fastened there with sinew and old rope, God in the body of a woman, and the fire does not consume her so much as *wear* her, the way a soldier wears his wounds like medals pinned by an idiot king.

I saw her in the field after the battle. The crows had already made their parliament of the dead, black robes gathered on the ribcages of horses, debating in their guttural Latin who owned the softest eyes.

And she burned.

Her hair was the smoke of seven villages. Her mouth opened and out came the sound of a portcullis dropping, the *chunk* of iron teeth into stone, and behind that sound, softer, the mewling of every child pulled from every mother since the first mother learned to grieve.

The bush that held her was crowned with thorns of course—*of course*—but also with the small skulls of birds, with rusted arrowheads, with the milk teeth of saints. It did not burn. Only she burned. Only she, ever, only her.

Look how her skin blackens and peels back like the pages of an illuminated manuscript thrown into a hearth, each curl of ash a saint's face going dark, each ember a gilt letter losing its gold to the greedy air.

She wept and her tears were boiling lead poured from the murder-holes above a gate, and where they struck the mud they hissed and set like the seals on a treaty no one intended to keep.

*Come closer,* she said, and her voice was a trebuchet, was the swing and release, was the impossible arc of a stone that hangs at the top of its flight forever, deciding.

I came closer.

I saw that the ropes binding her were her own veins, drawn out and knotted, that she had tied *herself* to this burning, that the war was inside her body like a swallowed sword, hilt-deep, and the point coming through her back as a flag.

And she smiled the way a wound smiles when you open it wider to clean it.

*This is what I am,* she said. *A woman on fire in a field of dead men, and no one puts me out, and no one lets me finish burning. This is mercy. This is what you asked for when you asked for me.*

The crows lifted all at once, a single black lung exhaling, and in the space they left I saw the whole world was the bush, and the bush was her, and she was burning, burning, tied to herself with her own blue rope, and would burn until the last of us learned to say her name without reaching for a sword.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a violent medieval painting in dense, poetic prose—horses with riders, women in danger, fire in the distance—using unusual similes and dark imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sacking

Look how the horses churn, their flanks lathered white as drowned men's faces, nostrils flared like the mouths of split pomegranates weeping seed. The riders hunch above them, iron-shouldered, their lances angled with the cold indifference of clock-hands measuring out a doomed hour.

The paint has trapped the smoke mid-crawl—a grey animal slouching across the far hills, where fire blooms orange as a fever behind the eyes. That distant burning sits patient as a tumor, feeding on some village whose name the artist never learned, whose people are already only ash arranging itself into rumor.

Nearer, the women scatter like startled psalms flung from a dropped book. One kneels with her hair unspooling black as spilled ink, her hands raised not in prayer but in that useless human gesture, palms out, as though tenderness alone could stop a blade. Her mouth is a small dark room where the scream still lives, unfinished, sealed forever in pigment and slow varnish.

A child clings to her skirts like a barnacle to a sinking hull.

The composition tilts everything toward ruin—diagonal, greedy, the way water leans toward the drain. Even the sky participates, bruised purple and yellow, the color of a wound three days old. Somewhere a banner falls, its heraldry snuffed like a candle pinched between wet fingers.

And the whole scene glows with that terrible varnished calm museums love: the violence lacquered, hung, admired—suffering turned to décor, screaming rendered *tasteful*, the dead posed prettily as fruit in a bowl gone soft.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic piece imagining what a chaotic religious/war scene looks like, full of strange comparisons involving time, insects, blood, and red hair.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Reliquary of Small Wars

*After a painting that may not exist*

---

Look how the hour bleeds sideways here—time does not march in this canvas but *swarms*, minutes crawling over the fallen like ants dismantling a beetle, patient and terrible, carrying away the seconds in their mandibles.

At the center, a saint or a soldier (the paint refuses to say) throws back a head crowned in red hair—no, in *flame*, no, in the specific russet of a fox caught mid-leap, that copper that looks like rust looks like the memory of blood before blood has finished happening. The strands lift as though gravity has taken the day off to attend some other massacre.

And the blood itself: it does not pool. It *ticks*. Each drop a small clock winding down, arranging itself across the flagstones in the numeral of some hour we have already survived and will survive again. The wound keeps its own liturgy.

See the horses—their eyes are wet with the panic of things that cannot pray. A banner tears. A censer swings its smoke like a slow gray insect testing the air for God. The mouths of the dying open in the shape of hymns their lungs can no longer afford.

Everywhere the small industries of catastrophe:
a locust of arrows,
a wasp-nest of shields,
a beetle-black boot filling slowly with the red-haired light of evening,
and time, always time, laying its eggs in the open wounds of the composition.

The painter has signed nothing. Perhaps because the scene is not finished. Perhaps because it is always finishing—each viewer another minute, another ant, another copper hair caught burning in the varnish, carrying a fragment of the ruin out through the museum door and into the merciful, forgetful street.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose poem where the narrator sees God as a naked burning woman, mixing themes of gender, violence, mortality, and decay.
counterfactuals.output:
# Apocrypha of the Burning Woman

She comes to me without clothing because clothing is a thing that ends, and She does not believe in endings the way we do—we, who fold our dead into boxes, who dress corpses for a party they will sleep through.

*

I saw Her first in the space between two heartbeats, that small failure, that stutter. Naked. Burning. Not a woman as men have carved women—not smoothed marble, not the obedient curve—but a woman as fire is a woman: consuming, unowned, refusing the vessel.

Her skin was the color of a struck match one second before the flame. Her hair was every animal I have watched die on a roadside, made luminous, made worthy.

*

*Are you God?* I asked.

She said: *I am what you do to God. I am the wound you have been praying into.*

*

Consider: they told me God was Father. A beard like weather. A hand that either blesses or breaks and calls both love. But here She stood, and every scripture I had swallowed came back up as ash, and in the ash I read the truer name—

that the divine has been female all along and we have been burning Her for it, century by century, a stake in every town square, a fire we mistook for holiness.

*

She let me touch the burning. This is the part I cannot explain to the living.

My hand went in and did not blister. My hand went in and I felt every woman who had gone into the flame before me—the healers, the widows, the ones who spoke too plainly, the ones who owned land, the ones who simply grew old and inconvenient—

and they were not screaming.

They were *speaking.*

*

*Why fire?* I asked Her.

*Because you cannot possess what is already leaving,* She said. *Because decay is only fire that has learned patience. The rot in the fruit, the rust on the blade, the softening of your own beloved face—all of it is Me, taking back what I lent. Slowly. Tenderly. Without asking.*

*

I have seen violence done in the name of a clothed God, a covered God, a God kept decent.

But this God bares Herself and the baring is the mercy. Look, She says. Look at the thing you fear. The body that ages. The body that bleeds on a schedule the moon dictates. The body that will one day be soil, be worm-work, be the black patient richness under someone else's garden.

You called this ugliness.

I am here to tell you it was God.

*

She is burning still. In the compost. In the hospice light. In the mirror where I watch my own hairline of gray advance like a slow and holy frost.

I no longer look away.

*

When I die—and I will, She promised it, the only honest promise ever made to me—I want to go into Her the way the wood goes: gratefully, giving off light, becoming for one bright moment the very thing that ends me.

Naked.

Burning.

A woman at last, whatever I was before.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness poetic description of a nightmarish medieval battle canvas, ending with a burning town and horses whipping ashes.
counterfactuals.output:
The Field Unmaking

Iron rain, iron rain, and the sky a bruise the color of old prayers—
banners drown here, swallowing their own colors,
red bleeding into the mud that was a meadow yesterday,
that was a wedding-path, that was nothing, that was a name.

Look how they lean, the men, into each other
like lovers who forgot the shape of tenderness,
pike-forest, spear-thicket, the wet percussion of it—
a jaw goes one way, a boy goes another,
his hands still open as if to catch the falling,
to catch the sun, to catch the mother-word
that never finished crossing his lips.

And the mud drinks. The mud is patient.
The mud has always known it would win.

Somewhere a trumpet, thin as a broken tooth,
calls a charge no one answers,
and the horses—God, the horses—
roll their moon-white eyes at the theology of steel,
foam-flecked, screaming a language we abandoned,
their great hearts drumming against the certainty of arrows.

A knight face-down, his visor a chalice for the rain.
A hand without an owner, still clutching.
A crow already, opportunist priest,
delivering last rites with its beak.

The smell—do you smell it?—copper and shit and smoke,
the trinity of every field where kings did their arithmetic
and counted us as coins.

Beyond the ridge the town is opening like a rose of fire,
each thatched roof a struck match,
and the bell tower tolls itself hoarse before it swallows flame,
before the whole horizon becomes a single throat of light.

The living flee. The dying stay. The mud keeps score.

And through it all the horses come again,
riderless now, mad with the perfume of ending,
hooves striking the char, hooves whipping the gray remains
of houses, of harvests, of the small warm hours of ordinary people—
ash rising in their wake like the last exhale of a world,
ash, ash, and the horses running through it,
running nowhere, running still,
whipping the ashes into the shape of everything we burned.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
